text: I"ve decided to update my review and change my recommendation, with caveats... .....I thought this would be a fun, relaxed sort of puzzle game. The mechanics are simple. The environment and music are pleasant. .....If you play the Ambient levels, it is exactly that. A fun enjoyable experience that moves at a comfortable pace. Puzzles range from easy to moderately hard but not frustrating. .....The Sentient levels however are a different story. .....In the Sentient levels you are competing against AI organisms that are very difficult to overcome. You have to Alt-Z a LOT to get a freshly generated map, in the hopes that you will get a starting point that gives you some chance of winning. And even then winning may depend heavily on luck. Expect to restart a LOT. .....The Force levels are frustrating but not as much as the Sentient levels. With more time I think I can find my peace with them. But thus far I have not been willing to invest the effort. After all, this was supposed to be a game that would allow me to relax and just have a bit of fun. .....So, if you want what the game advertises; a  relaxing ethereal sort of distraction with some challenging puzzle aspects, Play and Enjoy the Ambient levels and the beginner levels of the other two trees. .....If you are looking for a more difficult challenge that retains the basic playability of the ambient levels, try the more advanced Force levels. .....If you are a sadist, enjoy beating your head against a wall, and relying largely on luck to win, go for the upper Sentient levels. .....In the end, my recommendation comes down to whether or not I would buy the game again. Considering the price (I paid like $3.99 for it) I would say yes. It is an enjoyable game IF you stick to the modes you like. But I would not have paid full price for it.

text: It's a really nice, little game. The pixel art is interesting through adding little effects here and there, like how the background is always moving, yet it's not distracting. It makes a cool visual. The game's setting has an oddly not-so-desolate, metroid-like, planet as a setting, which I'm also a big fan of. Another thing I enjoyed was that all the NPC's were nice little guys, and came some interesting lines, if you went the distance to talk to them. The soundtrack is also really nice, it fits the space theme without being boring. The puzzles (stages that have you use a portal gun to advance) were difficult, but never so hard that I gave up. That was a big one for me, and it probably had to do with how well you could see the puzzle in whole, and the simple mechanics. I really love the puzzles. The story is... not very exisistent. There is some bad guy, Grigori (ugly fellow), who is a total jerk, he blew up your ship, you wreck, so now you have to find him on this planet you wrecked on (I don't know why the bad guy is there, I think we were trying to go to the planet to attack him, buy it's not well explained). It does provide an objective, but it isn't very complicated. In whole, I bought the game for $0.16 (an awesome price), and was surprised. However, the game is really short. My 3 hours were all I needed to beat the game. But, if you're okay with short games, it's a lovely experience. I was only upset at the length to be honest. It feels incomplete,  like a greenlight game. I really want more cool puzzles and funny creatures, but then the games over. I also beleive that with more time it could have a neat little plot to help tie the story together. I just want more. An update with a story that goes somewhere (maybe to other planets) would solve all my issues with this game. There are collectables and an achievement for completing the game under an hour, which make the game more replayable in its defense, but it just won't fill the void.

text: This game is an improvement over Overlord 1, but there's a critical flaw: the puzzles in it are terrible. A good puzzle is where you have all the pieces you need to start and get an "ah ha!" moment when you put them together. In this game puzzle pieces are such that when you find how they fit together, it's more of a "really? that's the solution?" A lot of the difficulty is telling apart the parts of the terrain you're supposed to interact with from the parts that are just fluff. "Oh, so that one vine I can send minions up, despite every version of that vine up to this point just being a decorative piece." Also, minions get stuck A LOT, and when a minion gets stuck then you're down a minion for the rest of the level. This means that by the time you get to the end, half your minions are stuck on terrain and you have to try to beat the boss with just a few minions. Note: If minions die, you can easily replace them. If they get STUCK, you're screwed.

title: overlord ii
text: A frustrating mix of great concept and terrible execution. I can't tell if I had more fun than controller-hurling rage. Every challenge is a wall of invulnerable guards that you get past by positioning a horde of reds at just the right spot to take out the captain. Sometimes you get to use a catapult or ballista. Strategy is fairly irrelevant. Every game has bugs, but it's the design choices that will drive you batty. What should have been a simple set of menus accessed from a keypress is instead a vast dungeon with rooms spread to the far corners, where your slow-walking avatar must trudge too, then wade through pointless "elevator" animations, and then even more animations before you can interact with the ungangly UI to manage a single resource. We're supposed to feel like we're entering a whimsical world, but mostly you just cry when you realize you have to trudge back across the entire dungeon to perform an upgrade. The magic system could have been completely removed without any loss to game play. You get four spells. You'll see a tutorial once. Then the spells seem to work by context, but despite a lot of experimentation, I couldn't figure out what the parameters were. I suspect it requires very precise targetting and timing that is more likely to happen by chance than by intent. But when you do get a spell to work, the effect is so underwhelming that it never seems worth the bother, and you certainly don't need them to complete the game, nor do they make it any easier. Then you get awarded women as trophy mistresses. It's just as shallow and pointless as it sounds.

title: papers, please
text: 10/10 Papers, Please is one of the best indie games I’ve ever played. It presents a nice challenge and plenty of moral dilemmas on each play through. There are dozens of possible endings and you will really want to play through more than once. It will take you a couple hours to complete the game the first time but I found myself coming back multiple times to try for different endings. The game is challenging and becomes almost overwhelming (but that’s the point). It reminds me a lot of games like Carmen Sandiego where you have to play close attention to small details and never turn off your brain.

title: papers, please
text: One of the most unique games I have played in a long time. A very easy to learn puzzle game of sorts, where you take the place of an employee at a border checkpoint. There isn't really much actual puzzle solving outside of some "side quests" that appear throughout the game, you spend most of your time scanning passports and entry slips for discrepencies. The pacing of the game is excellent, starting you off with just 1 document to look over, but throughout your time spent in Arstotzka regulations will change and your desk will be flooded with papers for each new person you see. The game becomes a race against the clock as you check over stamps and personal information to admit or deny entry without making mistakes. With mistakes come penalties to your daily earnings, which will quickly make it very difficult for you to keep your family safe and healthy. An interesting story that is changed by a combination between choices you make and your performance definitely adds some serious replay value to this game. You can continue your progress from any point to change decisions and uncover more of the 20 different endings available. The only complaints I have are the "upgrades" in the game are poorly executed, there are only 4 total, one even overrides the purpose of another. Also because of the art style it can be dificult to match faces to small pictures, leading to some misplays later in the game. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone regardless of what type of gamer they are.

text: One of the most enthralling yet basic games I've ever played. It's so simple in nature, but the allegory is deep and moving. While the game itself is relatively short (3-4 hours) there are many different paths to success and failure so it takes quite a bit longer to discover all the endings and achievements. Despite being an indie adventure simulation game, I found myself excited to role play as the Inspector and found much joy in doing so. If you buy this game, don't forget to have your paperwork on hand. Glory to Arstotzka!
